query: Which material can be used for superconducting properties, and why?

generation.hypothesis: An equiatomic refractory high-entropy alloy (HEA) that includes superconducting elements such as Nb and Ta (e.g., NbMoTaW) can exhibit superconductivity at cryogenic temperatures. This behavior arises because, under controlled processing conditions, short-range chemical ordering within the disordered BCC matrix may reduce electron scattering and enhance electron-phonon coupling, enabling Cooper pairing.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-principal element refractory HEA synthesized in a disordered BCC solid-solution state (e.g., equiatomic NbMoTaW) prepared by methods such as arc melting or additive manufacturing.
generation.intervention: Perform low-temperature resistivity measurements along with first-principles electronic structure calculations to assess superconducting ordering tendencies and critical temperature.
generation.conditions: Testing in a cryogenic environment (temperatures lowered to 1.5–10 K) ensuring phase stability, with controlled processing to maintain equiatomic composition and optimal short-range ordering.
generation.structural_mediator: Short-range chemical ordering in the BCC lattice, which may locally reduce disorder-induced electron scattering and foster effective electron pairing.
generation.mechanism: The mechanism is proposed to be electron-phonon mediated Cooper pairing. The presence of superconducting elements like Nb and Ta, when arranged with sufficient local order in a disordered alloy, enhances electron pairing due to reduced scattering and favorable electronic density-of-states.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under cryogenic conditions, the alloy will show a transition to a zero-resistance state below a critical temperature (estimated in the range of 5–10 K), indicating robust superconductivity.
generation.baseline: At temperatures above the superconducting transition, the material displays metallic behavior with finite resistivity.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for equiatomic or near-equiatomic compositions under carefully controlled synthesis such that the beneficial local ordering is present. Excessive compositional deviations or processing-induced disorder may prevent the superconducting transition.
generation.uncertainty: The exact critical temperature, the superconducting volume fraction, and detailed coherence lengths remain uncertain until experimental validation. In addition, the specific role and extent of the short-range ordering in supporting superconductivity requires further exploration.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize an equiatomic refractory HEA such as NbMoTaW using controlled processing (e.g., arc melting or laser-based additive manufacturing). Fabricate samples and perform four-point probe resistivity measurements while cooling from 20 K down to 1.5 K. Complement measurements with magnetic susceptibility tests (to check for the Meissner effect) and first-principles calculations of the electronic density-of-states and electron-phonon coupling constants.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the synthesized HEA does not exhibit a transition to zero resistivity or fails to show clear signs of the Meissner effect at temperatures below 10 K, the hypothesis that the material exhibits superconductivity due to favorable short-range ordering in the BCC structure will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have excellent mechanical properties, which could make them the substitutes of some superalloys. However, the high melting point of refractory HEAs leads to processing problems when using traditional processing techniques. In this study, a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW alloy was formed by selective laser melting (SLM) with a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. The composition distribution was analyzed, and the element with a lower melting point and lower density showed a negative deviation (no more than 5%) of the molar ratio in the formed alloy. The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys, making it a new substitute metal with great application prospects in aerospace and energy fields.

Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. decision.trend: None of the earlier papers address superconductivity or zero-resistance phenomena; they are focused on high-entropy alloys’ mechanical, thermal, and oxidation behaviors but do not investigate their superconducting properties. Research so far has centered on refining microstructures and improving mechanical or oxidation performance. Consequently, there is a clear gap concerning comprehensive studies of superconducting transitions within these multi-principal element materials.
decision.unsolved: Which specific high-entropy or other alloys, under what structural or thermodynamic conditions, might exhibit robust superconductivity remains unaddressed in these prior studies. No references here measure or optimize the zero-resistance transition temperature or examine the electronic structures needed for superconductivity.
decision.lever: Perform low-temperature resistivity measurements on promising multi-principal element alloys (e.g., equiatomic refractory HEAs) while using first-principles calculations to identify superconducting ordering tendencies and critical temperatures. Key parameters include controlled cryogenic testing down to ≤10 K and high-fidelity electronic structure modeling to link short-range order with superconductive phase formation.
decision.why: Since no published work in the set addresses superconductivity, a coordinated experimental and computational study is the most direct path to uncovering zero-resistance behavior in these alloys and clarifying their electronic structure–property relationships for superconductivity.
